concerns.message: Finding 3 never says which player a `covered` rule applies to. It reads "Within one step, for each type … the first targeted request (by `requestId` order) is answered `sighting`, and any other request for the same type in that step is answered `covered`". requestIds are global across players and outcomes come back as one flat list, so a literal reading ranks all players' requests for a type together. If player A and player B both buy a Moon rumor in the same step, B's request would be answered `covered`. B gets no message and pays nothing, even though B has not been told anything. Every test the task names uses one player, so this would pass every check.
concerns.consequence: A legitimate paid request from a second player quietly returns nothing. The general reviewer would most likely block for it, which means a fourth follow-up run. The fix is to say "for each (player, type)" in finding 3 before the worker starts.

concerns.message: Finding 1's "the same step with the triggers reversed" only works for triggers of one kind. The accumulator runs in a fixed order: losses first, then journal replacements, then targeted requests. A mixed sequence like storm loss, sun replacement, moon request therefore can't be reversed without changing which trigger has which type. Losses come from diffing held types, probably in preset type order. Replacements come from the journal's order inside the state, which a caller can't permute. Targeted requests are the only trigger a black-box test can reorder. With the new requestId ordering, merely reversing the requests array may not change the order in which they join at all. That would make the scripted test pass trivially without proving anything.
concerns.consequence: The worker writes a test that only reverses the requests array, and it proves nothing about losses, replacements or where sector choice draws the RNG. The coverage reviewer would then block on the same finding a fourth time. Name the permutable inputs: the requests array with requestIds swapped as well as the array reversed, the world-view arrays (players, rubbings, held types), and the journal and pending arrays if they are arrays. Or test the accumulator's pure add and emit helper directly, over all 3! orders. Compare outcomes sorted by requestId and `hashState`, not only messages.

concerns.message: The new permutation property can fail for reasons unrelated to the accumulator. Suppose the property generator emits two requests with the same requestId but a different player or type in one step. Which one is processed and which is answered `duplicate` then depends on array order. Candidate lists built in world-view array order and then indexed by an RNG draw also depend on order. Snapshot entries stored in world-view order do too.
concerns.consequence: The property check fails, or the worker narrows the sampled steps until it passes, and the proof gets weaker. Settle a within-step tie-break for a repeated requestId: first by payload, or answer every copy `duplicate` except the smallest in a canonical order. Also sort candidates by a stable key (sector index, then type) before any RNG pick.

concerns.message: `covered` is defined only for the case where the type actually appears in an emitted message. The plan doesn't say what the second and later same-type requests get in three cases: a capped step, a step where the type is ineligible (the older snapshot has no entry for it except the requester's own), and a free type that is in the accumulator but drops out at emit. If the code decides `covered` from accumulator membership instead of what the message contains, a request can be answered `covered` while nothing is delivered.
concerns.consequence: Outcomes are inconsistent, for example `capped` and then `covered`, or `covered` with no entry. Charging is still safe, but the coverage and general reviewers are likely to flag it. State that `covered` only applies when that player's emitted message contains the type. Otherwise every request for the type gets the first request's non-charged result (`capped` or `none`).

concerns.message: The double-charge fix only covers carrier sightings. A player can still pay 25 gold, answered `rumor`, for a type in the same step that a free fresh rumor after a loss already covers with a journal rumor. Two paid `rumor` requests for the same type in one step are also both charged, and may point to the same island. The general reviewer's finding was that paid rumors can be charged for information the player already gets, which applies to rumors as well as sightings.
concerns.consequence: The general reviewer may reopen the same finding on the rumor path. If it is out of scope on purpose, write that into decisions.md, for example: "covered applies to sightings only; a paid journal rumor can name a different target".

concerns.message: Finding 4 makes `validateIntelRules` refuse a reveal that isn't a multiple of the interval. The property runs use hand-built compressed configs, and nothing says they must pass the same validation. With the real constants, 33,600 ticks is 56 × 600, which is aligned. A compressed config that isn't aligned would keep testing a configuration that is now invalid. Or, if the configs do go through validation, the property tests would start throwing.
concerns.consequence: Either the tests keep exercising a split between pending and new sightings that production can't reach, or existing tests fail after finding 4 and need their expectations changed. Require every test config to pass `validateIntelRules`, and list any compressed config that had to be realigned in the report.

structured_output.simpler_alternative: Make order independence true by construction rather than something only tests show. Build each player's step in three phases. First, gather every trigger into a set keyed by (player, type), whatever order the triggers arrive in. Second, decide each (player, type) entry from the older snapshot: sort its candidates by a stable key, then draw the sector either from a key derived from (seed, snapshot tick, playerId, type) or from the shared RNG in sorted (player, type) order. Third, answer targeted requests grouped by (player, type) and sorted by requestId: `covered` if a free trigger put the type in the emitted message, otherwise `sighting` for the first and `covered` for the rest, or every request gets the same non-charged result. Then test the phase-2 and phase-3 helpers directly over all orders of three triggers across three types with two or more carriers each. Keep a single black-box property check that permutes the requests and world-view arrays and compares messages, outcomes sorted by requestId, and `hashState`. That test is about 20 lines, and it proves the property for losses and replacements too, which a black-box test can't reorder.
structured_output.cheap_experiment: Before the worker writes anything, restore the snapshot. Then write one throwaway scripted step at a snapshot boundary: one player, Storm, Sun and Moon each carried by two other players in different sectors, and three targeted requests. Run `stepIntel` twice: once with requests [storm r1, sun r2, moon r3], and once with the array reversed and the requestIds swapped as well (storm r3, sun r2, moon r1). Diff the messages and `hashState`. Then look at where `step.ts` (lines 400–490) draws the RNG for a sighting's sector. If the draw happens when a trigger is added instead of at emit, or indexes candidates in world-view order, the fix needs a code change and not just tests. That decides between phase 1 as a test-only change and the three-phase refactor. Next, add a second player requesting Moon in the same step and check that both players get `sighting`. That settles the per-player scope of `covered` right away.
